questions.question: Why is scope creep called the most under-monitored failure mode?
options: Each touch had a plausible reason in the moment; together they form a different change than was reviewed
It only happens when a scope contract on disk is missing its forbidden_files glob field entirely
The verification gate silently downgrades every block-severity finding into a mere warning note
It occurs only when two separate agents happen to edit the same repository during one shared working session
questions.explanation: Agents narrate each step in good faith; the silent total is the creep.

questions.question: Which contract field does the lesson call half the contract?
options: task_id, since it links the contract back to the board entry the human filed
forbidden_files (the negative space); a contract without it is incomplete
approvals_required, since every field above it depends on this one being set
rollback_plan, since the checker cannot run without a paragraph describing it
questions.explanation: A contract without forbidden_files is incomplete; the negative space is half the contract.

questions.question: Why pin allowed/forbidden to globs rather than raw paths?
options: Because raw paths cannot be stored as valid JSON string values in a contract
Real repos move files between sessions; globs like app/**/*.py survive refactors
Because glob patterns compress smaller than an equivalent list of raw paths
Because the scope checker only accepts glob syntax and rejects literal paths outright
questions.explanation: Globs (app/**/*.py) keep the contract valid through refactors.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say a contract needs a rollback_plan?
options: Rollback plans are required by the verification gate's schema validator
Without one, the checker cannot compute which files are in scope
Rollback plans let the agent skip acceptance criteria if something breaks
Writing it forces the author to think through what could go wrong first
questions.explanation: The lesson says listing how to roll back forces the contract author to think about what could go wrong; a contract you cannot roll back from should not be approved.

questions.question: What does the scope checker compare against the diff, per the lesson?
options: Only the commit message, checked against a required template
The task's estimated time budget against the actual wall-clock time
The allowed globs, forbidden globs, and any acceptance commands
The diff size in lines against a fixed per-task ceiling value
questions.explanation: The lesson says the checker reads the diff, the allowed globs, the forbidden globs, and a list of any acceptance commands that ran; each violation is a tagged finding.

questions.question: What must be true of feature_list.json before a session may start, per the lesson?
options: Every feature must already have a done_when line filled with output
At most one feature may carry status in_progress at any given time
The active feature must match the branch name exactly to proceed
At least one feature must be marked blocked before work may start
questions.explanation: The lesson says the invariant 'at most one in_progress' is itself a startup check: if the list shows two, the session refuses to start until a human resolves it.

questions.question: How does an agent pick which feature to work on, per the lesson?
options: It asks the human operator to assign one at the start of every session
It works through features strictly in the order they appear in the file
It picks whichever feature has the shortest done_when description
It picks one todo feature and cannot start a second in that session
questions.explanation: The lesson says the agent picks exactly one feature whose status is todo, writes its id into the active scope contract, and is forbidden from starting a second feature in the same session.
